slos.text: Define and calculate specific heat. theory
Suggest experiments to measure the specific heat capacity of a solid and of a liquid.
Analyze everyday effects due to the large specific heat of water. theory examination. Thermal Expansion and Kinetic Theory of Matter:
Use the terms for the changes in state between solids, liquids and gasses [including deposition and sublimation]. theory examination.
Explain thermal expansion in terms of kinetic theory for solids, liquids and gasses. [This includes stating the relative order of magnitudes of the theory expansion of solids, liquids and gasses].
Analyze the applications and consequences of thermal expansion in real life. theory examination.
Analyze melting, solidification, boiling and condensation in terms of energy transfer without a change in temperature. theory examination.
State the melting and boiling temperatures for water at standard atmospheric pressure. theory examination.
Describe qualitatively the thermal expansion of solids [linear and volumetric expansion]. theory (1 period=40
Explain the thermal expansion of liquids [real and apparent expansion]. theory Gases, Pressure, and Thermal Expansion

Analyze the pressure and the changes in pressure of a gas in terms of particles. [The forces exerted by particles colliding with surfaces, creating in final examination a force per unit area]. Changes in State:
Differentiate between boiling and evaporation. theory examination.
Describe evaporation in terms of particles [in terms of the escape of more energetic particles from the surface of a liquid]. theory examination.
Analyze how temperature, humidity, surface area and air movement over a surface affect evaporation. theory examination.
Explain how evaporation causes cooling. theory examination.
Describe the use of cooling caused by evaporation in the refrigeration process without using harmful CFCs. theory examination.
Explain latent heat [as the energy required to change the state of a substance and explain it in terms of particle behavior and the forces between particles].

Justify experiments to determine latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization of ice and water [including illustrating the analysis of data by sketching temperature-time graph on heating ice].
State that certain materials, when cooled to near absolute zero, can exhibit superconductivity. teaching

Describe superconductivity [as when atoms are in this state, their kinetic energy is low, so there is little (or no) resistance to the flow of electrons]. (1 period=40 examination, teaching Modes of Heat Transfer:
Justify experiments to distinguish between good and bad thermal conductors. theory examination.

Explain thermal conduction in all solids [in terms of atomic or molecular lattice vibrations and also in terms of the movement of free (delocalized) asked in final theory electrons in metallic conductors].
Explain convection in liquids and gasses [in terms of density changes]. Justify experiments to illustrate convection. theory examination.
Explain convection in seawater to support marine life. asked in final theory examination.
Describe the role of land breezes and sea breezes in maintaining moderate coastal climates. theory examination.
Explain how birds are able to fly for hours without flapping their wings and gliders are able to rise by riding on thermal currents. theory examination.
Describe the process of thermal energy transfer by radiation. [And know that it does not require a medium]. theory examination.
Describe the effect of surface color and texture on the emission, absorption and reflection of infrared radiation. theory examination.
Justify qualitatively how the rate of emission of radiation depends on the surface temperature and surface area of an object. theory
Justify Experiments to distinguish between good and bad emitters and absorbers of infrared radiation. theory examination. (1 period=40
Analyze the consequence of heat radiation in the greenhouse effect and its effect in global warming. theory examination.

Analyze everyday applications of conduction, convection and radiation [Including: (a) heating objects such as kitchen pans (b) heating a room by convection asked in final (c) measuring temperature using an infrared thermometer examination. (d) using thermal insulation to maintain the temperature of a liquid and to reduce thermal energy transfers in buildings (e) the mechanism of a household hot-water system]
Prove that waves transfer energy without transferring matter. asked in final theory examination.
Describe what is meant by wave motion. [As illustrated by vibrations in ropes and springs and by experiments using water waves]. theory Ask examination.
Describe the features of a wave. [in terms of wave front, wavelength, frequency, time period, crest (peak), trough, compression, rarefaction, theory amplitude and wave speed].
Define the terms frequency, wavelength, and amplitude. theory (1 period=40 examination.
Recall and apply the equation wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v =fλ).

Illustrate that for a transverse wave, the direction of vibration is at right angles to the direction of the energy transfer. [Including giving examples asked in final such as electromagnetic radiation, waves on the surface of water, and seismic S- examination. waves (secondary).

Illustrate that for a longitudinal wave, the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of the energy transfer [including giving examples such asked in final as sound waves and seismic P-waves (primary)].
Describe how waves can undergo reflection, refraction and diffraction. theory examination.
Describe how wavelength affects diffraction at an edge. theory examination.

Analyze the phenomenon of tsunamis generated under the surface of water [in terms of underwater earthquakes/volcanic activity generating waves that increase in frequency and amplitude as they encounter increasingly shallow water].
Describe how wavelength and gap size affect diffraction through a gap. theory examination. Sound:
Describe the production of sound. asked in final theory examination.
Describe the longitudinal nature of sound waves. asked in final theory examination.
State the approximate range of frequencies audible to humans as 20Hz to 20000Hz. theory examination.
Justify why sound waves cannot travel in a vacuum. [Including describing experiments to demonstrate this]. theory examination. (1 period=40
Describe how changes in amplitude and frequency affect the loudness and pitch of sound waves. theory examination.
Describe how different sound sources produce sound waves with different timbres [including making reference to the shape of the traces on an asked in final oscilloscope].
Describe an echo as the reflection of sound waves. theory examination.
Justify simple experiments to show the reflection of sound waves. theory examination.
Illustrate a method involving a measurement of distance and theory examination.
State that the speed of sound in air is approximately 330-350m/s. theory examination.
Describe that, in general, sound travels faster in solids than in liquids and faster in liquids than in gasses. theory examination.
Define ultrasound as sound with a frequency higher than 20kHz. theory examination.
Illustrate and analyze the uses of ultrasound. [In cleaning, prenatal and other medical scanning, and in sonar (including calculation of depth theory or distance from time and wave speed)].
Illustrate the use of infrasound [e.g., by elephants in communication, and in the study of seismic activity]. theory examination.
Analyze the effects of noise pollution on the environment. theory examination.
Justify the importance of acoustic protection. asked in final theory examination. (1 period=40
Describe how knowledge of the properties of sound waves is applied in the design of buildings with respect to acoustics. theory
Explain the use of soft materials to reduce echo sounding [such as in classroom studies, and other public gathering buildings]. theory examination.
Explain, with examples, how sound can reflect, refract and diffract. asked in final theory examination.
Explain how sound is converted by the eardrum and nerves into electrical signals that are then interpreted by the brain. examination, teaching Geometrical optics
Define and use the terms normal, angle of incidence and angle of Reflection. theory examination.
Describe an experiment to find the position and characteristics of an optical image formed by a plane mirror. [Same size, same distance from mirror as object and virtual image].
Use the laws of reflection to solve simple optical problems. asked in final theory examination.
Define the terms normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction. theory examination.

Apply the qualitative principle that a wave refracts towards the normal when it slows down while entering a medium, and that it refracts away from the normal if it speeds up when it enters a new medium. [In the case the angle of incidence is zero, then the waves continue parallel to the normal].
Define and use the refractive index from a vacuum to a medium for light as c/v. theory (1 period=40
Define refractive index n as n= sin(i)/sin(r). Apply Snell’s law, ni sin (i) = nr sin (r) to solve simple problems theory + Application
Describe an experiment to show refraction of light by transparent blocks of different shapes.
Define the terms critical angle and total internal reflection. Theory and PBA
Derive the equation n = 1/sin (c). theory examination.
Apply the equation n = 1/sin (c) to solve simple problems. theory examination.
Describe experiments to show internal reflection and total internal reflection. theory examination.
Evaluate and illustrate the use of optical fibers [particularly in telecommunications, stating the advantages of their use in each context]. theory examination.
Analyze the action of thin converging and thin diverging lenses on a parallel beam of light. theory examination.
Define and use the terms focal length, principal axis and principal focus (focal point) theory examination.
Draw ray diagrams to illustrate the formation of real and virtual images of an object by a converging lens. theory examination.
Differentiate between real and virtual images. theory examination.
Define and calculate linear magnification [as the ratio of image length to object length; state and use the equation linear magnification = image length/object length].
Describe the use of a single lens a magnifying glass. theory examination. (1 period=40
Explain the dispersion of light by a prism. [Including the detection of nonvisible spectra by a thermometer]. theory examination.
State the traditional seven colors of the visible spectrum in order of frequency and in order of wavelength. examination.
Describe the use of a single lens as in various optical device a photographic enlarger. This includes drawing ray diagrams to show how each form an image]. teaching.
Draw ray diagrams to show the formation of images in the normal eye, a short-sighted eye and a long-sighted eye. theory
Describe the use of converging and diverging lenses to correct long-sightedness and short-sightedness. theory examination

Illustrate with examples how the biological eye processes color in various organisms. [a. role of rods and cones in the eye, along with the brain, in detecting light and discerning color in combinations of 3 channels (red, yellow, blue). b. know that different living organisms may see more and less colors e.g. the mantis shrimp has 12 channels of color and view ultraviolet light]. teaching.

State that extreme gravity from interstellar objects like black holes can cause light to bend (from the perspective of the observer) in a way that is analogous to a simple lens. [This is called 'gravitational lensing']. teaching
State that 'acoustic lenses' are made of materials and shapes that work to focus or diverge sound. examination, teaching (1 period=40
State that there are positive and negative charges. [And charge is measured in coulombs]. theory examination.
State that unlike charges attract and like charges repel. theory examination.
Describe experiments to show electrostatic charging by friction. asked in final theory examination.
Explain that charging of solids by friction involves only a transfer of negative charge (electrons). theory examination.
Explain how a conductor can be charged by electric induction and then "earthing”. theory examination
Describe examples where charging could be a problem e.g., lightning. theory examination.
Suggest how charging and discharging is used in the application of various devices [e.g. photocopier and electrostatic precipitator]. examination.
Describe an electric field as a region in which an electric charge experiences a force. theory examination.
State that the direction of an electric field line at a point is the direction of the force on a positive charge at that point. theory examination. (1 period=40

Analyze and illustrate simple electric field patterns. [including the direction of the field: (a) around a point charge asked in final (b) around a charged conducting sphere examination. (c) between two oppositely charged parallel conducting plates (end effects will not be examined)]
State examples of electrical conductors and insulators. theory examination.
Describe an experiment to distinguish between electrical conductors and insulators. theory examination.
State and use a simple electron model to explain the difference between electrical conductors and insulators. theory examination.
Explain how a lightning rod can protect humans. theory examination.
Explain electrical breakdown [it occurs when a strong electric field passes through a gas and causes its atoms to ionize]. theory examination.
State that Corona discharge and Lichtenberg figures are visible examples of electrical breakdown. theory examination.

Explain how lightning is generated [Including the below steps of formation: - through friction between the water molecules suspended in clouds in the case of thunderstorms, and from between smoke particles in the case of volcanic lightning - lightning streamers are created through the process of electrical breakdown and theory this provides a path for the electric current from one charged object to the other - in the case of cloud-ground lightning a strong electric field from the clouds induces an opposite net charge in the conducting material present in the ground, and when this field becomes strong enough it generates lightning streams that provide the path for cloud-to ground and ground-to-cloud discharge].

State that there are many kinds of atmospheric lightning [e.g., sprites, jets, elves, trolls, pixies, ghosts, ball lightning) that are still being (1 period=40 researched]. teaching. Electric current and Ohm’s Law
Define and calculate electric current. [Use the equation electric current = charge/time | = Q/t to solve simple problems]. theory
Explain electrical conduction [in metals in terms of the movement of free electrons]. theory examination.
State that current is measured in amps (amperes) and that the amp is given by coulomb per second (C/s). theory examination.
Differentiate between direct current (d.c) and alternating current (a.c). theory examination.
Differentiate between conventional and actual current. theory examination.
Justify and illustrate the use of ammeters [(analogue and digital) with different ranges]. examination, teaching
Define e.m.f. [as the electrical work done by a source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit. Use the equation (by a source) per unit charge E = W/Q].
Define p.d. (potential difference). [As the work done by a unit charge passes through a component. Use the equation p.d. = work done (on a component) charge V = W/Q to solve simple problems].
State that e.m.f. and p.d. are measured in volts and that the volt is given by joule per coulomb (J/C). theory examination.
Justify and illustrate the use of voltmeters. [(analogue and digital) with different ranges]. (1 period=40 examination, teaching.
Calculate the total e.m.f. where several sources are arranged in series. theory examination.
State that the e.m.f of identical sources connected in parallel is equal to the e.m.f. of one of the sources. theory examination.
Describe an experiment to determine resistance. [Using a voltmeter and an ammeter and do the appropriate calculations]. examination, teaching.
Define and calculate resistivity [Use for a wire, the direct proportionality between resistance and length, and the inverse proportionality theory between resistance and cross-sectional area].
Define and apply Ohm'’s law. [Including reference to constant temperature. Use the equation resistance = p.d./current R = V/I to solve simple problems].
Describe the effect of temperature increase on the resistance of a resistor [such as the filament in a filament lamp]. Theory examination.
Interpret current-voltage graphs. [Including for a resistor of constant resistance, a filament lamp and a diode]. Theory and PBA Circuit Diagrams:

Draw circuit diagrams. [with cells, batteries, power supplies, generators, potential dividers, switches, resistors (fixed and variable), heaters, thermistors (NTC only), light-dependent resistors (LDRs), lamps, motors, asked in final ammeters, voltmeters, transformers, fuses, relays, diodes and light-emitting diodes examination. (LEDs)]. (1 period=40

Use common rules regarding current and voltage distribution in circuits to solve problems. [specifically: (a) the current at every point in a series circuit is the same (b) the sum of the currents entering a junction in a parallel circuit is equal to the sum of the currents that leave the junction asked in final (c) the total p.d. across the components in a series circuit is equal to the examination. sum of the individual p.d.s across each component (d) the p.d. across an arrangement of parallel resistances is the same as the p.d. across one branch in the arrangement of the parallel resistances]
Calculate the combined resistance of two or more resistors in series. theory examination.
Calculate the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel. theory examination.
Calculate current, voltage and resistance in parts of a circuit or in the whole circuit. theory examination.
Describe the action of negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistors and light-dependent resistors. [Including explaining their use as input theory sensors].
Analyze the function of variable potential dividers in circuits. [Including using the equation for two resistors used as a potential divider R1/R2= theory V1/V2].
Justify and illustrate the use of color codes for resistors. asked in final theory examination. Electric Appliances and Transmission:
Describe the working of a diode. asked in final theory examination
Describe the action of a light emitting diode in passing current in one direction only and emitting light. theory examination
Describe and explain the action of relays in switching circuits. be asked in annual examination, teaching.
State common uses of electricity. [Including heating, lighting, battery charging and powering motors and electronic systems]. theory examination.
Justify the advantages of connecting lamps in parallel in a lighting circuit. theory examination. (1 period=40
Use the equation, power = current x voltage P = IV to solve simple Problems. theory examination.
Use the equation energy = current x voltage x time E = IVt to solve simple problems. theory examination.
Define the kilowatt-hour (kWh). theory examination.
Explain the need to choose components with suitable power ratings. theory examination.
Calculate the cost of using electrical appliances where the energy unit is the kWh. theory Examination

State common electric hazards that may be caused from malpractice and lack of maintenance. [specifically: a) damaged insulation (b) overheating cables (c) damp conditions (d) excess current from overloading of plugs, extension leads, single and multiple sockets when using a mains supply]
Explain the use and operation of trip switches and fuses and choose appropriate fuse ratings and trip switch settings. examination, teaching
Explain what happens when a live wire touches a metal case that is Earthed. theory examination.
Explain why the outer casing of an electrical appliance must be either non-conducting (double-insulated) or earthed. examination.
State that a main circuit consists of a live wire (line wire), a neutral wire and an earth wire. theory examination. (1 period=40
Explain why fuses and circuit breakers are connected into the live wire for the circuit to be switched off safely. examination, teaching
Explain why domestic supplies are connected in parallel. theory examination.
Explain the damage that electric shock could do to a human being. [In terms of burns, cardiorespiratory failure and seizures]. examination, teaching. Electronics:
Explain that electronic devices are built from digital logic circuits. [That can act as switches that can convert incoming voltage into binary theory electrical pulses of high and low (or 1 and 0)].

Explain that Boolean logic is the basis for converting analogue data to digital data [this includes knowing that ‘bit' is the smallest unit of data in theory computing; either 1 or 0. Eight bits make up a byte].
State in words and in truth table form, the action of logic gates. [Specifically of AND, OR, NAND, NOR and NOT. theory examination. (1 period=40
Identify the use of logic gates for security purposes. [e.g.; burglar alarm, fire extinguish etc]. theory examination.
Use circuit symbols for the logic gates. theory examination.
Identify in given problems how Boolean switches can be put into combinations that then allow them to achieve logical operations. examination, teaching
Describe the action of a bipolar npn transistor as a switch. be asked in annual examination, teaching

Explain that transistors are commonly used in digital devices because they are both economical and act as rapid-response switches. [To enrich this concept students should be given an overview of how with advances in engineering, the number of transistors that can be fit per unit area onto a circuit board has continued to increase dramatically; this has rapidly enhanced computing power. They also be given an overview of how - breakthroughs in quantum physics are causing a new revolution in computing that are enabling computers to make exponentially more logical operations per unit time than with traditional computers].

State that circuits that maintain their 'state’ after receiving an input can be said to exhibit 'memory' [Since they retain the effect of the last action upon them (this should be taught to them with the context provided that circuit systems that allow for logical processing and memory functions form the basis of programmable electronics)]. teaching (1 period=40

State that quantum computers are still in early stages of development, and have to overcome manufacturing challenges such core components only functioning at very cold temperatures that are at almost absolute zero. teaching
Compare analogue and digital electronics. theory examination. Electromagnetisms
Describe an experiment to demonstrate electromagnetic induction. theory examination.

Use the fact that the magnitude of an induced e.m.f. is affected by (a) the rate of change of the magnetic field or the rate of cutting of magnetic asked in final field lines, and (b) the number of turns in a coil, to solve simple electromagnetic examination problems.
Use the fact that the effect of the current produced by an induced e.m.f. is to oppose the change producing it (Lenz's law). theory examination
Describe how a.c. generators work [(Rotating coil or rotating magnet setup) and the use of slip rings and brushes where needed]. theory examination
Sketch and interpret graphs of e.m.f. against time for simple a.c. generators [Including relating the position of the generator coil to the peaks, troughs theory and zeros of the e.m.f].
Describe the pattern and direction of the magnetic field due to currents in straight wires and in solenoids. theory examination
State the effect on the magnetic field of changing the magnitude and direction of the current. theory examination
Describe how the magnetic effect of a current is used in relays and loudspeakers [Including giving examples of their application]. (1 period=40 teaching
Describe an experiment to show that a force acts on current carrying conductor in a magnetic field. [including the effect of reversing: (a) the current examination (b) the direction of the field]
State and use the relative directions of force, magnetic field and current. theory examination
Describe the magnetic field patterns between currents in parallel conductors and relate these to the forces on the conductors. [Excluding the Earth’s theory field].

State that a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field may experience a turning effect and that the turning effect is increased by increasing: (a) the number of turns on the coil theory (b) the current (c) the strength of the magnetic field
Describe the operation of an electric motor, including the action of a split-ring commutator and brushes. theory examination
State that it is theorized that the Earth's magnetic field is generated by the rotation of the Earth and it molten iron core that contains charged particles in motion. teaching
Explain the principle of operation of a simple iron-cored transformer. theory examination
Use the terms primary, secondary coils and step-up and step- down transformer. theory examination
Use the equation V p / Vs = Np /Ns [Where P and S refer to primary and secondary, to solve problems]. theory examination
Justify the advantages of high voltage transmission. [Including theory (1 period=40 explaining why power losses in cables are smaller when the voltage is greater].
Describe the deflection of an electron beam by electric fields and magnetic fields. examination, teaching
Interpret waveforms on oscilloscope. be asked in annual examination, teaching Electromagnetic Waves:
State the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and in order of wavelength. theory examination
State that the speed of all electromagnetic waves in: (a) a vacuum is 3.0 x 108 m/s theory (b) air is approximately the same as in a vacuum

Describe the applications of electromagnetic waves in society. [specifically: (a) radio waves: radio and television communications, astronomy (b) microwaves: satellite television, mobile (cell) phone, Bluetooth, 5 periods microwave ovens (c) infrared: household electrical appliances, remote controllers, be asked in annual alarms, thermal imaging, optical fibers examination, (d) visible light: photography, vision (e) ultraviolet: security marking, detecting counterfeit bank notes, sterilizing water teaching (f) X-rays: hospital use in medical imaging, security scanners, killing cracks in metal (g) gamma rays: medical treatment in detecting and killing cancerous cells, sterilizing food and medical equipment, engineering applications such as detecting cracks in metal] (1 period=40

Describe the damage caused by electromagnetic radiation. [Including (a) excessive exposure causing heating of soft tissues and burns and (b) ionizing effects caused by ultraviolet (skin cancer and cataracts), X-rays and gamma rays (cell mutation and cancer)]. teaching

Explain qualitatively, how scattering of light by molecules in the air give the sky its blue color during the day and its shades of red during sunset. theory [Use of the terms Rayleigh and Mei scattering are not required].

State that theoretically light can also be considered to be made of massless particles that carry energy and momentum called 'photons'. [Students should know as an example of this particle nature; light exerts pressure on objects (very slight) and this has been used by satellites that have 'solar sails' that accelerate with the help of force from light rays].

Describe the structure of the atom. [In terms of a positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electrons that go around the nucleus. This should include an understanding of the below big ideas: - These electrons do not go around in predictable circular paths in the way that planets go around the sun. be asked in annual The electrons behave as 'quantum particles’ and their location and momentum at examination, any point in time is governed by probability; one cannot predict the motion of an electron. - The 'shells' in which electrons ‘orbit' refer to the level of kinetic energy the electrons possess; the farther the shell is from the nucleus, the more energy the teaching electron has. - If one were to 'look' at an atom, one would see a fuzzy 'cloud' of electrons with a very small nucleus in the center (akin to a football with flies around it in a boundary of several football fields)].

Justify the findings of the alpha particle scattering experiments. [Specifically, that it provides evidence for: (a) a very small nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space theory (b) a nucleus containing most of the mass of the atom (c) a nucleus that is positively charged]
Define the terms proton number (atomic number) Z and nucleon number (mass number) A and be able to calculate the number of neutrons in a theory nucleus. (1 period=40
Recall the term nuclide and use the nuclide notation z XA. theory examination
Explain what is meant by an isotope and state that an element may have more than one isotope. theory examination
Explain what is meant by background radiation. be asked in annual examination, teaching
State the sources that make a significant contribution to background radiation. [Including: (a) radon gas (in the air) (b) rocks and buildings (c) food and drink (d) cosmic rays].
Describe the emission of radiation from a nucleus as spontaneous and random. theory examination
Describe α-particles, β-particles and  -radiation. theory examination

Justify qualitatively the order of strength for α-particles, β- particles and  -radiation in terms of their asked in final (a) their relative ionizing effects examination (b) their relative penetrating powers
Describe the deflection of α-particles, β-particles and radiation in electric fields and magnetic fields. theory examination

Explain that radioactive decay is a change in an unstable nucleus that can result, most commonly [there are other kinds of decay as well but students asked in final are not required to study those at this level), in the emission of α-particles, β- examination particles and  -radiation]. (1 period=40
Use decay equations, using nuclide notation, to show the emission of α-particles, β-particles and y-radiation. asked in final examination

Describe nuclear reactions (fission & fusion) with examples [fusion as the formation of a larger nucleus by combining two smaller nuclei with asked in final the release of energy, and recognize fusion as the energy source for stars].
Apply the equation E = mc2 to calculate the energy released in the process of nuclear reactions. theory examination
Describe the activity of a radioactive material in terms of counts per unit time. theory examination

Define and infer the half-life of materials [Half-life as the time taken for half the nuclei of an isotope in any sample to decay. Use this definition of theory half-life in calculations, which may involve information tables or decay curves].
Explain and apply the concept of Carbon dating to solve problems. theory examination

Explain how the type of radiation emitted and the half-life of the isotope determine which isotope is used for applications: [including: (a) household fire (smoke) alarms (b) irradiating food to kill bacteria (c) sterilization of equipment using gamma rays (d) measuring and controlling thicknesses of materials with the choice of radiations used linked to penetration and absorption (e) diagnosis and treatment of cancer using gamma rays] used for applications
State the effects of ionizing nuclear radiations on living things, including cell death, mutations and cancer. examination, teaching

Explain how radioactive materials are moved, used and stored in a safe way. [(with reference to: (1 period=40 (a) reducing exposure time (b) increasing distance between source and living tissue (c) use of shielding to absorb radiation] teaching

Explain the nature of the Sun [as a star of medium size it consists mostly of hydrogen and helium, and that it radiates most of its energy in the infrared, visible and ultraviolet regions of the electromagnetic spectrum]. teaching
Describe that it is hypothesized that most of the matter in the universe is made up of dark matter. teaching Theory of Knowledge in Physics:
Explain how global warming contributes to extreme weather events. [Specifically in the case of hurricanes, heat waves, flooding, rainfall, asked in final wildfires, droughts and winter storms].

Explain the phenomena of geothermal activity on the basis of conduction, convection and radiation. [How magma flows beneath the Earth, why it causes tectonic plate movement, volcanic eruptions and how the center of the Earth remains hot since being formed over 4 billion years ago]. teaching Wave Theory:

Explain, with examples in Physics, falsifiability as the idea that a theory is scientific only if it makes assertions that can be disproven. teaching Benchmark |: Students should be able to follow provided safety instructions and take general precautions in a lab setting
